Who can register?
You must:
be a
South African citizen
;
be
at least 16 years old
(you can only vote from age 18); and
and have a
green, barcoded South African identity document (ID)
,
smartcard ID
, or a valid
Temporary identity certificate (TIC)
.
To Register within South Africa
When and where can I register?
Make an appointment to apply for registration during office hours at the
local IEC office
responsible for your voting district. Please always phone first to make an appointment.
Register to vote using our
Online Voter Registration Service
until the date of proclamation of the election. You can use our Voter Information Portal site to register to vote or update your current voter information, view your current address, request a special vote, find a voting location, view important election dates (upcoming election in your ward).
What documents do I need to apply for registration?
Whether you are registering online or in person, you must provide your South African ID, either:
Green, barcoded ID book, or
Smartcard ID, or
Valid Temporary Identity Certificate (TIC).
No other forms of identification are accepted. Only original documents from the
Department of Home Affairs
are accepted.
Where can a person register to vote?
a)
Online:
registertovote.elections.org.za
b)
At the voting station during national registration events.
c)
IEC Local Office (during office hours).
d)
During Targeted Communication and Registration (TCR) drive.
e)
During Civic and Democracy Education (CDE) events.
When does a person update their registration details?
A voter will be required to update their registration details if:
a)
the voter has changed their place of residence, i.e. has a new address;
b)
the voter has an incomplete or no address;
c)
a voter has been issued with a new ID number which is different from the old one;
d)
the Municipal Demarcation Board has changed ward boundaries;
e)
the Electoral Commission has changed the voting district boundaries;
How does a person check his/her voter registration status?
Voters may use the following facilities to check their registration status:
i.
WEBSITE
www.elections.org.za
ii.
ii. SMS ID number to
32810
iii.
Toll-free phone call from a landline to the call centre (
0800 11 8000
) -
only available during specific periods announced by the Commission
iv.
Online application on smart phone/laptop/iPad at
https://registertovote.elections.org.za
v.
IEC WhatsApp Chatbot (
060 088 0000
) – redirects to the website
vi.
Download our mobile app
and enter your ID number
vii.
vii. Voting Station [Registration Weekend]

Talking to people

Make A Submission On A Bill
Have Your Say
» Make A Submission On A Bill
The South African Constitution makes provision for public involvement in lawmaking, oversight and other processes of Parliament. South Africa’s democratic system not only provides for citizens to elect their representatives, but also allows citizens to have a say in matters that affect them.
One of the ways that the public can make their voices heard is by making submissions to the National Assembly Committees, the National Council of Provinces Committees or Joint Committees. For submissions from the public to be effective, content and format need to be considered carefully.
It is important that a submission is easily read and understood by the Members of committees.
View Calls for Submissions and Nominations
How To Make A Submission
WHAT IS A SUBMISSION?
A submission is the presentation of views or opinions on a matter or piece of legislation under consideration by a committee of Parliament.
Submissions may be presented in your language of choice.
Submissions are usually in written form. They can be reinforced through oral representation to the committee, if the person or group who has made the submission is invited to make an oral presentation.
Making submissions creates an opportunity for any member of the public to propose changes or suggest possible actions to ensure that the laws passed by Parliament or any other matter being considered by Parliament, serve their purpose.
HOW TO WRITE A SUBMISSION?
While there is no set format for a submission to a committee, it should be well thoughtout and easy to read.
The following suggestions may help to achieve this:
Heading
– Head your submission with the name of the committee to which it is addressed and the full title of the Bill or topic.
Who is it from?
– Clearly state whom the submission is from. State your name or give the name of the organisation you represent.
Contact Details
– Include a contact address and daytime telephone number. If for private reasons you do not wish those details to be publicly released with your submission, state this in a covering letter and leave it off the submission itself.
Do you wish to appear before the Committee?
– Clearly indicate whether you would like the opportunity to address the committee in person. If you represent an organisation and you wish others to appear with you before the committee, either for support or to speak, include their names and roles.
Your organisation
– If you are writing on behalf of an organisation, give brief details of the organisation’s aims, membership and structure. Make sure that you have the authority to do so and note your position within the organisation.
Who else supports you?
– You may note how widely you have consulted during the writing of the submission. Your submission may have more standing if it has a wide support base.
GUIDELINES FOR WRITTEN SUBMISSIONS
When writing a submission to a committee, you will usually be making comments in relation to a Bill or topical issue. While there are differences in the way in which a submission is written for a Bill, there are basic principles that apply.
Language usage
– Use respectful language. A submission which uses slanderous and disrespectful language will not be considered.
Relevant
– Stick to the point. Your submission must be relevant to the matter being discussed. A committee may decide not to entertain a submission that is not relevant.
Clear
– Arrange your sentences and paragraphs in a logical order. Try to present a clear and logically developed argument. A submission that jumps from one issue to another and back again or mixes unrelated issues together may be confusing and decrease its impact.
Concise
– Be simple and direct. Do not write more than is necessary. An overly long submission may weaken the key points you wish to address. The committee wants to know what you think and the evidence or arguments you have that support your view.
Accurate
– Be accurate and complete. Gather and research all relevant information thoroughly. Make sure that your facts are correct. A submission with many errors will greatly reduce its impact.
Conclusion
– Sum up or list the main points of your recommendations in a conclusion at the end of the submission or in an executive summary at the beginning.
Sending your submission
– Your submission should reach the committee by or before the closing date for submissions, and should be sent to the relevant Committee Secretary.
PRESENTING ORAL SUBMISSIONS
Oral submissions give you a chance to reinforce what you have said in your written submission and allow the committee to clarify points raised in the submission. If the committee has decided to hear your submission, the Committee Secretary will contact you to make arrangements to hear your oral submission.
Oral submissions can also be made at Public Hearings held by Committees.
These submissions are recorded at the Public Hearing and transcribed.
The relevant Committee/s looks at the evidence or opinions shared at the Hearing and discuss the contents thereof.
If the view is supported by many people and if it has merit, the idea or concern stands a good chance of being included into the work of the relevant Committee/s.
The Committee/s will make the final decision about the merit of an issue.
GUIDELINES FOR MAKING ORAL SUBMISSIONS
The format for the presentation of oral submissions varies between committees and also depends on the nature of the business.
Follow the same guidelines as for written submissions.
Preparing for your oral submission
– As committee meetings are generally open to the public and the media, you may wish to attend one of these meetings before you present your oral submission. On the day of your oral submission, arrive early. It is a good idea to plan your presentation so that you are able to present all relevant points and leave enough time for questions.
Visual Aids
– Parliament’s committee rooms are fitted with audio-visual equipment and your oral submission may have more impact if it is reinforced with audio-visual aids.
Language
– You may present your oral submission in any of the official languages of South Africa. Inform the Committee of your language choice before the time so that Parliament may make the necessary interpreting arrangements.
Questions
– Be prepared for questions from Members of the Committee. It is a good idea to think about possible questions that may be asked and be prepared to answer them.
Time allocation
– You can discuss the amount of time allocated to you with the Committee Secretary, beforehand. The committee makes the final decision on the time allocated for oral presentations.
Take part in Parliament. Make your voice heard.

Have Your Say: The General Finance Laws Amendment Bill (B21-2026)
The Standing Committee on Finance invites stakeholders and interested parties to submit written submissions on the
General Finance Laws Amendment Bill (B21-2026)
The General Finance Laws Amendment Bill (B21-2026) aims to amend:
the Financial Sector Regulation Act, 2017
(Act No. 9 of 2017)
, so as to insert a Chapter to provide for the designation of replacement benchmarks; to provide for the effect of replacement benchmarks on legacy contracts; to provide for the limitation of liability arising from the selection or utilisation of a replacement benchmark or a designated adjustment spread; to provide for a consultation process for designations or determinations made by the Reserve Bank in relation to benchmark replacement; and
the Public Procurement Act, 2024 (Act No. 28 of 2024), so as to amend the timeframe within which the Minister must review the implementation of the Act, make a report public and submit such report to Parliament, and to provide for matters connected therewith.
Public hearings will be held on Tuesday, 13 October 2026.
Submissions must be received by no later than 12:00 on Monday, 12 October 2026.
Those who want to make presentations at the public hearings should specifically request this. The hearings will be conducted through Zoom.

Parliament, Friday, 18 September 2026 –
The Portfolio Committee on Employment and Labour has officially opened public comments on the
Employment Services Amendment Bill [B 16–2026]
, thereby initiating a critical step in formulating a legislation that will reshape South Africa’s labour migration framework.
The proposed Bill seeks to legally regulate the employment of foreign nationals amid shifting economic and demographic dynamics, a shift the committee believes needs to be shaped by views from all sectors of the South African society. Accordingly, the committee invites citizens, civil society, business formations, and organised labour to submit written input before formal parliamentary deliberations commence.
The Bill is also intended to, among other things, update the foundational Employment Services Act of 2014 by broadening its statutory enforcement powers and expanding legal protections to new sectors. A primary focus of the amendment is regulating foreign labour by introducing structured frameworks to manage the employment of non-citizens, ensuring total statutory alignment with the Immigration Act and the Refugees Act.
Stakeholders submitting written representations are requested to indicate if they wish to deliver a verbal presentation during upcoming parliamentary public hearings.

The Portfolio Committee on Employment and Labour has officially opened public comments on the
Employment Services Amendment Bill [B 16–2026]
, thereby initiating a critical step in formulating legislation that will reshape South Africa’s labour migration framework.
Media Statement
The proposed Bill seeks to legally regulate the employment of foreign nationals amid shifting economic and demographic dynamics, a shift the committee believes needs to be shaped by views from all sectors of South African society. Accordingly, the committee invites citizens, civil society, business formations, and organised labour to submit written input before formal parliamentary deliberations commence.
The Bill is also intended to, among other things, update the foundational Employment Services Act of 2014 by broadening its statutory enforcement powers and expanding legal protections to new sectors. A primary focus of the amendment is regulating foreign labour by introducing structured frameworks to manage the employment of non-citizens, ensuring total statutory alignment with the Immigration Act and the Refugees Act.
Stakeholders submitting written representations are requested to indicate if they wish to deliver a verbal presentation during upcoming parliamentary public hearings.

ATC261008: Report of the Portfolio Committee on Higher Education on the assessment of progress made in implementing the recommendations and resolutions of the P20 Youth Parliament, dated 7 October 2026
Higher Education
Report of the Portfolio Committee on Higher Education on the assessment of progress made in implementing the recommendations and resolutions of the P20 Youth Parliament, dated 7 October 2026
Having considered the progress made by the Department of Higher Education and Training (“the Department”) in implementing the recommendations and resolutions contained in the P20 Youth Parliament Report, the Portfolio Committee on Higher Education (“the Committee”) reports as follows:
1. Introduction and Background
On 3 December 2025, the Speaker of the National Assembly referred the Report on P20 Youth Parliament – 13 June 2025 for consideration and reporting in terms of National Assembly Rules 338, 339 and 340. On 16 February 2026, the Speaker of the National Assembly wrote to the Minister of Higher Education and Training to convey the resolutions on the Report of the P20 Youth Parliament adopted by the National Assembly (NA). The correspondence highlighted specific recommendations contained in the report that the Department was required to implement. These recommendations included the following:
The Department:
a) together with the National Student Financial Aid Scheme (NSFAS), should table annual reports on the ring-fenced funding for students with disabilities;
b) together with the Department of Employment and Labour, must strengthen oversight over Sector Education and Training Authorities (SETAS), Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) colleges, and artisan training centres to align with labour market needs and enforce graduate placement targets;
c) together with the Departments of Basic Education, Health, Social Development, Justice and Constitutional Development, and Police must submit quarterly reports on the national strategic plan (NSP) on Gender-Based Violence and Femicide (GBVF), with disaggregated data on youth survivors and related issues such as teenage pregnancies and statutory rape;
d) in collaboration with relevant departments, must support the development of sport-related career pathways through accredited programmes and practical placements. These initiatives must be costed and funded; and
e) together with National Treasury and other stakeholders, develop sustainable mechanisms to address the student debt crisis, especially for financially vulnerable students.
Subsequently, on 19 August 2026, the Committee convened a meeting with the Department, during which one of the agenda items was a progress report on the implementation of the recommendations and resolutions arising from the P20 Youth Parliament held on 13 June 2025.
2. Summary of the progress report presented by the Department of Higher Education and Training
The Department of Higher Education and Training (DHET) presented the progress made in implementing recommendations arising from the P20 Youth Parliament Report to the Committee. The report focused on improving student support, strengthening skills development systems, addressing gender-based violence and femicide (GBVF), expanding career opportunities, and responding to the student debt crisis.
2.1. Recommendation 1: Together with NSFAS, table annual reports on the ring-fenced funding for students with disabilities
The Department reported that disability funding currently comes from NSFAS's overall annual allocation of approximately R50 billion. Based on expenditure trends from 2023 to 2025, approximately R200 million of the total annual student budget allocation can be ringfenced for students with disabilities, with just over 80% for university students and 20% for Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) Colleges.
The Department supports the recommendation to introduce dedicated reporting on disability-related expenditure to improve transparency and accountability. Future annual reports will provide information on funding allocations and disbursements, the number of beneficiaries across universities and TVET colleges, expenditure categories, disability types supported, and the effectiveness of current funding arrangements.
2.2. Recommendation 2: Together with the Department of Employment and Labour, must strengthen oversight over SETAS, TVET colleges, and artisan training centres to align with labour market needs and enforce graduate placement targets
The Department reported significant progress made through the TVET College Connectivity Project. The Project has established a national digital platform supporting blended learning and expanded Wi-Fi access across 142 TVET college campuses. It has improved ICT infrastructure, strengthened cybersecurity, and enhanced network support through SANReN. It has also contributed to building institutional capacity through asset transfer, staff training and technology investments.
Furthermore, the Department indicated that support is being provided through the National Open Learning System (NOLS), a digital platform serving universities, TVET colleges, and Community Education and Training (CET) colleges. The platform currently offers more than 200 courses and has over 32,000 registered users. Strategic partnerships with organisations such as HP, Microsoft and Intel have strengthened digital skills development, lecturer training, and Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) initiatives, including artificial intelligence laboratories within TVET colleges.
To support infrastructure development, the Department noted that the Capital Infrastructure and Efficiency Grant (CIEG) have allocated R1.292 billion over the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework period. These funds will be used to support the development of workshops, ICT infrastructure, bulk municipal services, and health and safety upgrades to provide a safe, efficient and fit-for-purpose teaching and learning environment across the TVET sector.
The Department also noted that it strengthened artisan development through the successful implementation of the Dual-System Apprenticeship Model under the Centres of Specialisation Programme. Occupational programmes are designed in collaboration with industry partners, and 57 workshops have been modernised through an investment exceeding R300 million. Lecturer professional development and workplace placements have further enhanced training quality, contributing to improved employability and trade test success rates.
In collaboration with the Department of Employment and Labour, the Department is also strengthening SETA oversight. Skills Branch performance indicators for SETAs focus on employer partnerships for workplace-based learning opportunities, increased internship and apprenticeship placements, tracer studies to monitor graduate employment outcomes, and contributions toward the national target of producing 22,000 artisans are key performance targets during the 2026/27 financial year.
2.3. Recommendation 3: Together with the Departments of Basic Education, Health, Social Development, Justice and Constitutional Development, and Police must submit quarterly reports on the national strategic plan (NSP) on Gender-Based Violence and Femicide (GBVF), with disaggregated data on youth survivors and related issues such as teenage pregnancies and statutory rape.
The Department indicated that data on youth survivors, teenage pregnancies and statutory rape are not comprehensively available within the Post-School Education and Training (PSET) system, as some of this information falls within the reporting responsibilities of the Department of Basic Education. Nevertheless, it indicated that substantial interventions are underway.
During 2025, TVET Colleges, CET Colleges and universities recorded extensive engagement in GBVF awareness, risk assessments, counselling services, referrals, and pregnancy-related support. The Department continues to implement prevention programmes through Higher Health initiatives, including civic education, peer education programmes, and curriculum integration within TVET colleges.
The Department indicated that it is also conducting awareness campaigns, policy implementation workshops, and institutional monitoring to strengthen GBVF prevention and response mechanisms. Particular focus is placed on providing psychosocial support, ensuring access to referrals and protection services, addressing discrimination, supporting LGBTQIA+ students and staff, and promoting inclusion for students with disabilities.
2.4. Recommendation 4: In collaboration with relevant departments, must support the development of sport-related career pathways through accredited programmes and practical placements. These initiatives must be costed and funded
To support career opportunities in sport, the Department incorporated 26 sport-related occupations into the National Career Advice Portal (NCAP). The platform provides detailed career information, including job descriptions, admission requirements, qualifications, learning pathways, professional registration requirements, and further study opportunities. Multimedia content, including career videos, has been developed to enhance student awareness and career guidance.
2.5. Recommendation 4: Together with National Treasury and other stakeholders, develop sustainable mechanisms to address the student debt crisis, especially for financially vulnerable students.
The Department noted that it recognises student debt as a significant barrier to equitable access and success in higher education and presents a significant financial sustainability challenge for institutions. It noted that addressing the challenge requires a coordinated whole-of-government approach involving the Department, National Treasury, NSFAS, public universities, private sector, and other strategic partners. Key interventions include conducting a sector-wide assessment of student debt to determine the scale and causes of indebtedness, examining the demographic profile of indebted students, and analysing institutional debt patterns. The Department is also engaging the National Treasury on sustainable funding mechanisms that strengthen the student financial aid system, including policy options for supporting the "missing middle" and students who require limited additional support to complete their studies.
Additional measures were put in place to address student debt, which include accelerating the finalisation of NSFAS close-out and reconciliation processes, strengthening data integration and financial oversight, expanding affordable student accommodation through public-private partnerships, implementing accommodation cost caps, and finalising a regulatory framework to manage fee increases at public universities.
The Department is further exploring innovative debt-relief mechanisms through partnerships with SETAs, development finance institutions, philanthropic organisations, and private-sector stakeholders. Collectively, these interventions aim to reduce financial exclusion, improve student success, strengthen institutional sustainability and create a more equitable and sustainable funding system.
3. Key observations from the discussion
Having considered the progress made by the Department of Higher Education and Training in implementing the recommendations and resolutions contained in the P20 Youth Parliament Report, the Committee made the following key observations:
3.1. The Committee noted the Department’s response to the recommendations but expressed concern about the underreporting of GBVF cases and the inadequacies in the management of such cases across the PSET system.
3.2. The Committee further noted that GBVF is linked, in part, to the shortage of safe and suitable student accommodation, particularly in rural areas. Therefore, the Department is urged to explore public-private partnership models to expand student accommodation and ensure that students’ mental health support needs are considered in the planning and development of such facilities.
3.3. The Committee recalled its earlier request to Higher Health to develop an application-based reporting system that would enable students to report GBVF incidents and access mental health support services across the PSET system. The Committee expressed concern that the application has not yet been developed, noting that the delay hampers efforts to strengthen reporting mechanisms and improve the effective management of GBVF cases.
4. Recommendations
Having considered the progress made by the Department of Higher Education and Training in implementing the recommendations and resolutions contained in the P20 Youth Parliament Report, the Committee recommends the following:
4.1. The Department and NSFAS should present the funding allocations and disbursements for students with disabilities to the Portfolio Committee on Higher Education. Furthermore, NSFAS should ensure that future annual reports provide information on the number of beneficiaries across universities and TVET colleges, as well as budget allocation.
4.2. As part of the mechanisms to curb GBVF, the Department of Higher Education and Training, in collaboration with relevant stakeholders, develops and implements a comprehensive strategy to expand the provision of safe and suitable student accommodation, particularly in rural and underserved areas, through public-private partnership initiatives.
4.3. Higher Health should develop an application-based reporting system that would enable students to report GBVF incidents and access mental health support services across the PSET system.
Report to be considered.

Executive Undertakings and Petitions
REPORT OF THE EXECUTIVE UNDERTAKINGS AND PETITIONS COMMITTEE ON A PETITION FROM ZILANDANA COMMUNITY CALLING FOR PARLIAMENT TO INVESTIGATE FAILURE OF THE KUMKANI MHLOTLO LOCAL MUNICIPALITY TO CONSULT THE COMMUNITY DURING THE 2025/2026 WARD DEMARCATION PROCESS, DATED 23 SEPTEMBER 2026.
1. INTRODUCTION
The Committee received a petition from the Zilandana Community in the Balasi Administrative Area, Kumkani Mhlontlo Local Municipality, Eastern Cape, concerning the ward delimitation process. The petition was referred by the Speaker to the National Assembly on 14 May 2026. The petitioners raised concerns regarding public participation and the possible impact of the new ward boundaries on community cohesion, representation and access to municipal services.
The Constitution in Section 56 (d) and 69 (d) provides for petitions to be brought to Parliament. It provides for the National Assembly (NA) and the National Council of Provinces (NCOP) to receive petitions, representations or submissions from any interested persons or institutions. Chapter 14 of the Rules of the National Assembly (9th edition), Rule 337 (d) makes provision for the Speaker.
2. BACKGROUND
Following the referral of the petition, the Committee met on 10 June 2026 for the purpose of tabling and considering the petition. A brief analysis of the petition was presented to the Committee, following which the Committee resolved that correspondence be addressed to the relevant government stakeholders to obtain responses to the issues raised in the petition.
Initial correspondence was addressed to the relevant stakeholders on 19 June 2026, requesting their responses to the matters raised in the petition. Follow-up correspondence was subsequently issued in respect of outstanding responses on 14 July 2026.
In a letter dated 1 July 2026, the petitioner informed the Committee that positive and constructive engagements were taking place between the Zilandana community and the relevant stakeholders and requested that the parties be afforded an opportunity to continue with these engagements.
The matter was subsequently brought before the Committee on 5 August 2026, as part of the consideration of responses received from the relevant stakeholders. Having considered the responses and noted the progress made through the engagements between the parties, the Committee resolved to conclude and close the petition. The Committee further resolved that the petitioner be informed of its decision and be requested to provide the Committee with updates on the engagements and progress between the parties every six months.
In accordance with the Committee's resolution, a letter dated 6 August 2026 was addressed to the petitioner, informing him of the Committee's decision to conclude the matter and requesting updates every six months on the ongoing engagements. The petitioner subsequently indicated his agreement with the Committee's approach and was requested to provide a formal written response.
A formal response from the petitioner, dated 24 August 2026, was received by the Committee, confirming his agreement to the proposed arrangement.
3. STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT AND RESPONSES
The Eastern Cape Department of Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs, OR Tambo District Municipality and Kumkani Mhlontlo Local Municipality engaged directly with the Zilandana community. The Municipal Demarcation Board (MDB) also provided information on the statutory ward delimitation process.
The MDB confirmed that the prescribed consultation and objection processes had been followed and that the final ward configuration had been submitted to the Electoral Commission for the 2026 Local Government Elections. It further indicated that the ward boundaries could not be amended outside the next statutory delimitation cycle.
Kumkani Mhlontlo Local Municipality undertook to strengthen community participation by holding selected Council meetings within rural communities and ensuring that ward arrangements do not negatively affect service delivery or community participation.
4. COMMITTEE DELIBERATIONS AND FINDINGS
The Committee noted that its intervention facilitated engagement between the Zilandana community and the relevant government institutions.
The Committee further noted that the community had been afforded an opportunity to raise its concerns and that the engagements were constructive and satisfactory. The petitioners indicated that they understood that the current ward boundaries could not be amended during the existing delimitation cycle and expressed their intention to participate in the next public participation and ward delimitation process. The Committee noted the commitments made by the Municipality to strengthen rural community participation and access to municipal decision-making.
5. RESOLUTION
The Committee resolved to:
· note the responses and engagements undertaken by the relevant stakeholders;
· note the petitioner’s satisfaction with the engagements and the progress made;
· regard the matter as resolved and close the petition; and
· note that the petitioner will provide the Committee with regular updates on the engagements and progress every six months.
6. CONCLUSION
The Committee is satisfied that the concerns raised in the petition received appropriate consideration and that positive and constructive engagements took place between the community and the relevant stakeholders. The Committee therefore considers the petition resolved and closed. The Committee considered and adopted the report during its meeting held on 23 September 2026.

Public Accounts (SCOPA)
Report of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts on its hearings with local municipalities (Masilonyana Local Municipality and Msunduzi Local Municipality) held in May 2026, dated, 30 September 2026
1. Introduction
The Standing Committee on Public Accounts (SCOPA) identified municipalities as a priority focus area in its five-year strategic plan for the 7th Parliament. This decision was informed by the persistent concerns raised in the 6th Parliament legacy report, as well as the critical role of local government in delivering essential services to communities. In response, the committee resolved to intensify its oversight of local municipalities to strengthen financial accountability and improve service delivery outcomes.
The Auditor-General of South Africa (AGSA) briefed the Portfolio Committee on Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (PC on COGTA) and SCOPA on the audit outcomes and financial affairs of local municipalities. The briefings took place on 08 May 2026.
The joint committees also received a briefing from the Special Investigating Unit (SIU) on 29 April 2026 on the status of investigations conducted under all relevant proclamations pertaining to these local municipalities.
Subsequent to these briefings, the joint committees conducted formal hearings with the municipalities in May 2026.
2. Governance of local municipalities
The municipalities in South Africa are governed by a distinct structure guided by the Municipal Structures Act 117 of 1998, the Municipal Systems Act 32 of 2000, and the Municipal Finance Management Act 56 of 2003 (MFMA), operating on a separation of powers framework. Together, these key statutes define the legal categorisation, operational structures, service delivery mechanisms, and financial accountability standards for local government. The municipal council serves as the primary governing body holding both legislative and executive authority, responsible for approving policies, budgets, and bylaws. Executive authority is led by the Executive Mayor/Mayor, who appoints Members of the Mayoral Committee (MMCs) to oversee specific portfolios, provide political leadership, and drive policy implementation. The Municipal Manager/City Manager acts as the head of the administration and the accounting officer, tasked with daily management, executing council direction, ensuring fiscal accountability, and managing senior staff.
To enforce oversight and accountability, the Municipal Public Accounts Committee (MPAC) interrogates financial reports, investigates unauthorised, irregular, fruitless and wasteful expenditure, and recommends disciplinary or corrective actions to council.
Both Masilonyana and Msunduzi local municipalities face operational, governance, and financial crises that severely compromise their ability to deliver essential services. Financially, both institutions experience revenue collection challenges, mounting debt burdens, and widespread non-compliance with supply chain management regulations resulting in increased balances of unauthorised, irregular, fruitless and wasteful expenditure. Operational delivery is heavily crippled by crumbling, poorly maintained infrastructure, leading to utility distribution losses in both water and electricity. At a structural level, both municipalities exhibit significant human resource vulnerabilities marked by prolonged leadership vacancies and widespread staff non-compliance with minimum qualification requirements, alongside a breakdown in internal consequence management where oversight bodies fail to enforce timely disciplinary action.
Due to persistent non-compliance, unfunded budgets, non-payment of bulk suppliers (Eskom and Water Boards) and third parties, escalating unauthorised, irregular, fruitless and wasteful expenditure, and a lack of consequence management, the National Treasury took a decision in July 2026 to invoke Section 216(2) of the Constitution to temporarily withhold equitable share allocations, Masilonyana Local Municipality is one of the affected municipalities. While funds were later conditionally released to prevent basic service disruptions, National Treasury emphasised that strict compliance requirements, including signed creditor payment plans, reduction of unauthorised, irregular, fruitless and wasteful expenditure balances, and disciplinary actions remain in force to enforce long-term financial accountability.
3. Masilonyana Local Municipality
Masilonyana Local Municipality appeared before the Committee on 26 May 2026. The municipality has been characterised by severe administrative dysfunction, poor record-keeping, and financial instability. During the 6th Parliament, the Committee conducted an oversight visit from 22 to 24 August 2022 and adopted the oversight report with recommendations on 28 September 2022. The Committee found serious weaknesses in governance, financial management, service delivery, record-keeping, project management, revenue collection, Supply Chain Management (SCM), and consequence management. Key recommendations made included conducting a skills audit, strengthening internal controls, improving SCM controls, development, and monitoring of audit action plans, and improving oversight over infrastructure projects.
The joint committees PC on COGTA, together with SCOPA and the Standing Committee on the Auditor-General (SCOAG), conducted a joint oversight visit to the Free State Province on 24 and 25 July 2025. In respect of Masilonyana Local Municipality, the committees reported similar findings to those of the previous oversight visit, indicating that there is no improvement, as persistent governance and financial management challenges, including consecutive disclaimer audit opinions, weak consequence management, poor financial controls, an unfunded budget, water and sanitation challenges, and concerns regarding leadership instability and accountability. The report was adopted by the PC on COGTA on 09 September 2025 and required the provincial executive and the municipality to report on corrective actions to address these challenges.
Furthermore, Masilonyana Local Municipality is one of the municipalities that were referred to the Speaker of the National Assembly by the AGSA due to challenges relating to the non-submission and auditing of annual financial statements, which required parliamentary oversight intervention. The matter was subsequently referred to SCOPA, and on 19 March 2025 the committee received a briefing from the AGSA on municipalities with outstanding or late annual financial statements. During the briefing, the AGSA highlighted Masilonyana Local Municipality's persistent late submission of annual financial statements, which resulted in a material irregularity being issued against the municipality. The AGSA also raised concerns about ongoing weaknesses in financial management, governance and service delivery, while the committee emphasised the need for improved accountability, oversight and corrective actions.
Following a resolution by the Free State Provincial Executive Committee on 17 December 2025, the provincial government officially placed Masilonyana Local Municipality under section 139(1)(b) of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa, effective from 01 February 2026. The decision to place the municipality under administration was informed by governance failures, financial distress, and inability to fulfil statutory service delivery obligations.
3.1 Audit outcomes
The municipality has experienced nine consecutive years of disclaimer audit opinions, from 2016/17 to 2024/25 financial years, with repeat findings on non-compliance with Municipal Finance Management Act (MFMA) as the municipality regularly fails to meet statutory deadlines on the submission of financial statements, procurement and contract management, expenditure management, utilisation of conditional grants, revenue management, asset management, consequence management, human resource management, and performance management.
3.2 Achievement of planned targets
The municipality’s performance and planning reporting mechanisms suffer from critical control deficiencies, legislative non-compliance, and disconnection between budget and reported achievements. The AGSA reported that the Annual Performance Report (APR) lacked the required prior-year comparisons, target-to-indicator linkages, and corrective action plans, while key performance indicators were inconsistent, unmeasurable, and missing supporting evidence. Prolonged leadership vacancies further hindered effective in-year monitoring.
The municipality only achieved 45 per cent of its overall basic service delivery targets, with key water, road, and electrification infrastructure projects completely stalling. The following key indicators were not met; the refurbishment and upgrading of the Winburg portable water treatment works by 30 June 2025, the target was 9 and the achievement was 0; for the construction of the Winburg/Makeleketla portable water pipeline from Sedibeng reservoirs by 30 June 2025, the target was 8 and the achievement was 0; for the quarterly reports on grading 5 km of roads across four towns by 30 June 2025, the target was 4 and the achievement was 0; for the quarterly reports on the electrification of 210 stands in Makeleketla/Winburg by 30 March 2025, the target was 2 and the achievement was 0; and for the 11KV strengthening of the Winburg/Makeleketla switching station by 31 December 2024, the target was 6 and the achievement was 0.
3.3 Revenue collection
The municipality faces critical revenue collection challenges, marked by a massive debt burden and consistently low collection rates. The municipality informed the Committee that as of 31 March 2026, total municipal debtors reached R2.1 billion, with a low monthly average collection of R5.3 million, reflecting an overall collection rate of just 19 per cent. Performance across recent financial years highlights ongoing billing and recovery challenges. In 2022/23, the municipality billed R187.08 million and collected R29.21 million (15.6 per cent), in 2023/24, collection slightly improved, R182.66 million was billed and R48.74 million was collected (26.7 per cent), however, in 2024/25, the collection rate dropped significantly to 14.3 per cent, of the R339.05 million billed, only R48.51 million was collected. The municipality attributed the low collection rate to high local unemployment, defective billing systems, illegal connections, and meter tampering, weak debt enforcement, and failure to regularly issue monthly customer accounts.
The committee raised concerns on the low collection rate and enquired how the municipality finances its daily operations, to which the municipality replied that because revenue collection falls far short of operational expenses, it relies heavily on its equitable share grant of R157 million annually, just to meet payroll obligations, leaving no operating budget for basic municipal services.
3.4 Unfunded budget
The AGSA reported that the municipality operated on an unfunded budget, highlighting a persistent failure to align operational expenditure with realistic revenue generation. A primary driver of this severe structural deficit is a profound imbalance between municipal income and baseline payroll obligations. The municipality informed the Committee that it operates on a monthly salary bill of roughly R14.4 million to R15 million, while its own monthly revenue collection ranges between only R1.8 million and R2 million. This vast discrepancy, coupled with optimistic revenue assumptions, leaves the municipality without the cash flow needed to cover basic budgeted commitments.
3.5 Irregular expenditure
The irregular expenditure increased from R11.929 million in 2023/24 to R47.438 million in 2024/25, mainly due to non-compliance with procurement and SCM regulations. The closing balance at the end of the 2024/25 financial year was R159.841 million, the entire balance (100 per cent) remained unchanged and unaddressed, with no recoveries, condonements or write-offs.
The municipality attributes this to the non-functionality of crucial oversight bodies like the MPAC, which was entirely inactive in previous years and has convened only once since taking office to address Unauthorised, Irregular, Fruitless, and Wasteful (UIFW) expenditure. The AGSA issued a qualification on completeness of irregular expenditure, therefore the amount disclosed is not a true reflection of the actual expenditure.
3.6 Fruitless and wasteful expenditure
The municipality incurred fruitless and wasteful expenditure of R15.660 million for the 2024/25 financial year, which represents a significant increase from R6.829 million in 2023/24, due to interest charged on overdue supplier accounts. The closing balance at the end of the 2024/25 financial year was R46.711 million (2023/24: R31.111 million). None of the fruitless and wasteful expenditure has been addressed by the municipality, as there were no recoveries, condonements or write-offs. Furthermore, fruitless and wasteful expenditure was not investigated as required by section 32(2)(b) of the MFMA.
3.7 Going concern - events and conditions
The AGSA reported on the going concern status of the municipality, highlighting severe financial instability and operational risks. Included in the comparative figures for contingencies is R97 million owed to third parties, including R75 million owed to a pension fund that was cleared from the register based on an active repayment agreement, though necessary payment reconciliations and supporting audit documentation were not provided. In addition, concerns remain that National Treasury could recover unspent conditional grants as it did previously, threatening delay or halt critical infrastructure restoration. Furthermore, the AGSA noted severe underinvestment in assets as evident, with expenditure on repairs and maintenance at just 1.3 per cent of total property, plant, and equipment valued at R971.333 million. Finally, the municipality faces an acute debt crisis, owing Eskom R253.665 million against annual electricity sales revenue of only R25.334 million.
3.8 Electricity and water losses
The municipality suffered substantial utility distribution losses due to technical faults, and ageing infrastructure resulting from inadequate routine repairs and maintenance. Electricity distribution losses amounted to R20.462 million in 2024/25 (2023/24: R8.755 million). Similarly, water distribution losses amounted to R7.143 million (2023/24: R5.802 million), resulting from defective water meters and widespread network leaks.
3.9 Procurement management and deviation
During the 2024/25 financial year, the municipality reported deviations from SCM regulations totalling R110 419, which included R85 459 for exceptional cases where standard procedures were impractical, R17 673 for emergency procurements, and R7 287 for single-source suppliers. However, the AGSA’s findings on procurement and contract management revealed far broader systemic non-compliance, including uncompetitive and unfair procurement processes linked to deviations amounting to R1.6 million across 3 instances.
3.10 Infrastructure projects
The AGSA audited two primary infrastructure projects, the Refurbishment of Masilo/ Theunissen Wastewater Treatment Works (WWTW), funded by the Water Services Infrastructure Grant and the Upgrading of the Sewer Pump Station and Outfall Sewer in Winburg / Makeleketla, funded by the Municipal Infrastructure Grant. Welcome to the Eastern Cape Provincial Legislature's website! This site provides a ready reference to information and news about the Eastern Cape Provincial Legislature.
The Eastern Cape Provincial Legislature (ECPL), situated in Bhisho, is the provincial legislative power. The Eastern Cape Provincial Legislature is a people's assembly that upholds democracy and transparency and is committed to uplifting the life of the people in the Eastern Cape by effectively administering its constitutional obligations.
It is important to know how the Legislature works, because it belongs to you; the people of our beautiful province. You voted for a political party to represent you in the Provincial Legislature; therefore MPLs have the responsibility of ensuring that you are informed of all aspects within the province that affect you, your family or your community. You need to know how, when and where you can participate and influence the decisions that are taken in the Legislature.
This means that the Legislature must be open and accountable. It means that ordinary people must be able to see and hear what is happening here. It means that you must be able to meet your public representatives and ask them about the work that they are doing to ensure a better life for you. You also have the responsibility to voice your support or disapproval on issues that affect your daily living. Tell the MPLs about your problems that you face in your community. This is your right!

NORTH WEST PROVINCIAL LEGISLATURE
In the North West Province, we have 38 seats. The Presiding officers are the Speaker, the Honourable Ntsetsao Viola Motsumi, the Deputy Speaker, the Honourable Collen Maine and the Secretary, Advocate Ludendo Netshitumbu.
The current North West Provincial Legislature was established by the 1993 Interim Constitution of South Africa upon the creation of the new nine provinces. The 1993 Constitution came into effect (and the provinces came into existence) on 27 April 1994; the election on the same day elected the first Provincial Legislatures. For the most part, the Provincial Legislatures have been controlled by the African National Congress. The exceptions are the KwaZulu-Natal Legislature, which was controlled by the Inkatha Freedom Party from 1994 to 2004; and the Western Cape Provincial Parliament, which was controlled by the (New) National Party from 1994 to 2004 (sometimes in coalition with the Democratic Party) and since 2009 has been controlled by the Democratic Alliance.
HOW ARE MPLS ELECTED?
The Members of the North West Provincial Legislature (MPLs) are elected by party-list proportional representation with a closed list, using the largest remainder method with the Droop quota to allocate any surplus. Elections are run by the Independent Electoral Commission, and are held every five years, simultaneously with the elections to the National Assembly. Elections have been held in 1994, 1999, 2004, 2009, 2014 and 2019.
WHAT ARE THE POWERS OF THE LEGISLATURE?
The legislature has the power to pass legislation in various fields enumerated in the national constitution; in some fields the legislative power is shared with the National Parliament, while in others it is reserved to the province. The fields include such matters as health, education (except universities), agriculture, housing, environmental protection, and development planning. In fields outside the power of the North West Provincial Legislature, it may recommend legislation to the National Assembly.
The North West Provincial Legislature may also enact a constitution for that province, if two-thirds of the members vote in favour. The powers of the North West Provincial Legislature are bound only by the national constitution and the provincial constitution (if one exists). There is no provincial Constitution in the North West so it is bound by the national Constitution.
Why The Constitution?
The Constitution sets out rules governing the exercise of authority in the country, and it determines the powers which are given to government, as well as the limits to those powers.
“The Republic of South Africa is one, sovereign, democratic state founded on the following values:
(a) Human dignity, the achievement of equality and the advancement of human rights and freedoms.
(b) Non-racialism and non-sexism.
(c) Supremacy of the constitution and the rule of law.
(d) Universal adult suffrage, a national common voters roll, regular elections and a multi-party system of democratic government, to ensure accountability, responsiveness, and openness.”

Welcome to the Western Cape Provincial Parliament
The Western Cape Provincial Parliament (WCPP) is one of the nine provincial legislatures in South Africa.
Based in Cape Town, the WCPP is constitutionally mandated to pass legislation, provide a forum for public debate, involve the public in the law-making process, and oversee the activities of the provincial executive.
The WCPP consists of 42 Members, elected every five years on a proportional representation system. The Premier and members of the provincial Cabinet are appointed from these Members.
This website contains information about the role and function of the WCPP, news, parliamentary activities including sitting and standing committee meetings, Members of the Provincial Parliament (MPP), legislation, publications, career opportunities, etc.

Welcome From Speaker
Thank you for visiting our website. I am Daylin Mitchell, the elected Speaker of the Western Cape Provincial Parliament (WCPP).
Our website plays a crucial role as a one-stop information hub for all your parliamentary information needs. See what is happening at the WCPP by viewing our calendar or download one of our many publications, including all the Papers of the House, transcriptions of proceedings (Hansard) and educational material. You can also view the livestreams of the sittings of the House and committee meetings: simply click on ‘LIVE’ on the homepage.
Read More
Public participation is a vital component of the functioning of our parliament. Our focus is on building stronger relations with the people of the Western Cape to promote the essential role of active citizenship in the law-making processes. Our Public Education and Outreach team also presents educational workshops, either at our building or in communities. Feel free to contact them. You will find their details by clicking on the ‘Get Involved’ button on the left-hand menu.
The WCPP is also responsible for ensuring that the Executive of the Western Cape Government is held accountable for the spending of taxpayers’ money and for providing the necessary services. The WCPP fulfils this role by conducting vigorous oversight over the provincial departments through its standing committees.
Do you want to visit our institution? No problem! We provide tours for any persons wishing to learn more about our institution. Find details about visiting the WCPP by clicking on the ‘Visit Parliament’ button on the left-hand menu.
Please follow us on X, Facebook and YouTube by clicking on the icons below. For other enquiries, please feel free to contact us on the details provided at the bottom of this page.
Thank you for showing an interest in the work of this parliament. Together we can make a meaningful contribution towards improving the quality of life of all the people of the Western Cape. We will advance the causes of freedom, fairness and opportunities for all by encouraging a diverse society through active citizenry. By making just laws and conducting quality oversight, we will promote and protect the rights of all people.

Comment on the review of the draft combined rules for Ward Committees
1 October - 31 October 2026
About
Ward Committees serve as an important participatory governance structure that facilitates communication and engagement between communities through the subcouncil.
They play a critical role in -
promoting community participation in municipal affairs,
identifying local needs and priorities, and
supporting the delivery of responsive and accountable local government.
To ensure that Ward Committees continue to function effectively and in accordance with current governance requirements, the City of Cape Town has undertaken a review of the existing Rules governing Ward Committees and has developed Draft Combined Rules for public consideration.
The review seeks to:

Enhance the effectiveness of Ward Committees in facilitating meaningful public participation.
Improve operational procedures and reporting obligations.
Ensure alignment with applicable legislation, policies, and best practices.
Your input will contribute towards the development of a comprehensive and streamlined set of rules that supports accountable governance, enhances community involvement in municipal affairs, and promotes effective collaboration between the City of Cape Town and the communities it serves.

About​​​​​​​
The City’s Urban Planning and Design branch has prepared a draft LSDF for the Kensington, Factreton and Wingfield areas, and we want your input.
The LSDF provides direction for short-, medium- and long-term spatial and investment planning in the Kensington, Factreton, Acacia Park, and Wingfield local areas.
The study area - bound to the South by the rail lines South of Maitland cemetery; to the East by the rail lines West of Maitland; the N1 in the North and Jakes Gerwel Drive to the East – has complex spatial planning conditions that we need to respond to, including:
Location:
access to employment areas, road and rail based public transport makes the area strategic and desirable for urban development. This area will change in meeting the demand as more people look for homes in the area
Affordable housing:
the residential areas have a mix of vulnerable households, informal settlements and homes that are rapidly increasing in value
Mixed development:
The mixed use and commercial area along Voortrekker Road is considered an accessible area suitable for redevelopment and intensification of all land
Urban regeneration:
Large, dispersed public land holdings require review as to how they can be developed and connect with the existing neighbourhood
The LSDF aims to:
Formulate a vision for the desired future of the area
Set key policies and guidelines for decision-making and actions
Coordinate, integrate and direct future development
The proposed vision is:
“A well connected and safe area for all. Where residents thrive and children can play freely in dignified and sustainable public spaces. An area providing access to high quality, secure and affordable housing. Where local businesses can prosper, offering work opportunities. A place of belonging and pride.”
The key objectives include:
safety and access,
social cohesion and housing,
sustainable urban growth,
service-led growth, and
biodiversity and open space.
